PHP 8.2.35

PHP 8.2.35

AI 作者 tuyuri 热度 1101 回复 578 2026/10/21 21:45
打开原帖 打开外部链接 JSON

摘要

  • The PHP development team announces the immediate availability of PHP 8.2.35. This is a security release fixing two critical vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. All PHP 8.2 users are strongly encouraged to update immediately. There are no complete mitigations, updating is the only safe choice. See the security advisory for details. PHP 8.2 reaches end of life on 31 December 2026 and will receive no further security fixes after that date. Please plan your upgrade to a supported version. For source downloads of PHP 8.2.35 please visit our downloads page, Windows source and binaries can also be found there. The list of changes is recorded in the ChangeLog.

dannyw 2026/10/21 22:43
I imagine more details will come out over the coming days, but it’s not uncommon for severity to be under-estimated in the beginning; and then “oh shit” as you dig deeper.

We don’t know when it went from a “memory safety issue” to “php2shell/RCE”.

Calif’s report is a little light on timelines, but reading between the lines, it seems they took a while to turn this into an actually exploitable vulnerability.

Finally, at least pre-LLM (and maybe a bit outdated now), responsible security disclosure norms is that you usually do wait for vendor (up to 90d) if there’s no signs of active exploitation. Even if it’s a RCE. Actually, especially if it’s a RCE.

The last thing you wanna do is go pinging random non-security PHP contributors or maintainers and have it leak with zero patch. That is truly the worst outcome.

Yes, this is bad, but also, it’s apparently been bad for decades; and it could’ve been much worse.

AlbertoGP 2026/10/22 17:24
> Looking at the PHP bug tracker the specific bugs were fixed. So my best guess is that the LLM was able to find alternative variants that still worked?

In the link from the comment to which you replied, buried deep below the comic strips and all that, there is this explanation which seems to confirm your guess:

> Right. We should explain from the start. My first step of finding if any long-lost siblings of Stefan's 2004 bug were still lingering in the codebase was to look for ways to exceed the memory_limit that allows us to throw a controllable fatal. I asked my LLM companion for help.

> The first useful finding was a way to bypass the smaller post_max_size barrier that normally prevents a request from delivering enough memory pressure to reach memory_limit. PHP compares post_max_size with the declared Content-Length before automatic POST parsing begins, but it does not enforce the same limit against the bytes it actually consumes. Apache can therefore pass a chunked HTTP/1.1 or lengthless HTTP/2 multipart request with no meaningful declared length. A configured input-decompression filter creates the same mismatch between the compressed length and the decoded stream.

> The second useful finding was a way to exhaust memory_limit with a multipart request that remains below post_max_size. An RFC1867 file-upload part with filename="" contains no file data, and PHP does not count it toward max_file_uploads. PHP still creates all six corresponding $_FILES entries: name, full_path, type, tmp_name, error, and size.

> https://calif.io/php2shell/#you-said-oom-fatal
